text.en: In July 1054, Chinese astronomers saw a new star; 12 days later came the schism in Constantinople. That star's remnant is the Crab Nebula.
Moscow is first mentioned in a chronicle in 1147 — around the time Angkor Wat was being completed in Cambodia.
Moscow is first mentioned in a chronicle in 1147. By then, teaching had been going on at Oxford for about half a century.
When Prince Igor marched against the Polovtsians in 1185, Notre-Dame had been under construction for 22 years. It would not be finished until the mid-14th century.
Eight years after Magna Carta, the princes of Rus first met the Mongols and were crushed on the Kalka River.
The Battle on the Ice (1242) came just four years after work began on the Alhambra in Granada (1238).
While Basil II was finishing off Bulgaria at Kleidion (1014), Rus' was getting its first law code, the Russkaya Pravda (1016).
1240: in summer Alexander beat the Swedes on the Neva; in December Batu took Kiev. Northern Rus' held off the West while the south fell to the East.

King Cnut ordered back the tide not out of arrogance but to expose it. In Henry of Huntingdon's 12th-century tale he sat before the rising sea, got his feet wet and told his courtiers that the power of kings is empty.
Domesday Book, the 1086 survey of England, got its name because it could not be challenged. As the treasurer Richard FitzNeal explained, there was no appeal from it, as from the Last Judgement.
Richard the Lionheart, an English icon, spent no more than six months of his ten-year reign in England. The rest went on crusade, in captivity or defending his lands in France.

'Assassin' comes from a nickname for a medieval order based in the Alamut mountain fortress in Iran, founded in 1090. Enemies called them hashishin; the tales of hashish before killings are widely doubted.

Legend says Sultan Mahmud promised Ferdowsi a gold coin per couplet of the Shahnameh, then paid in silver. The poet gave it to a bath attendant and a beer seller. When the remorseful sultan sent gold, Ferdowsi had died.

Al-Biruni measured the Earth by climbing a hill. Comparing the dip of the horizon from its top and from the plain in today's Pakistan, he got the planet's radius right to within about 2%, by one estimate.

The two great women of Japanese classical literature did not get on. Murasaki Shikibu, author of Genji, wrote that Sei Shōnagon of The Pillow Book was 'dreadfully conceited' and littered her writing with Chinese characters.
Japan's tea culture began with seeds in a monk's luggage. In 1191 Eisai came back from China with Zen teachings and green tea seeds, and is credited with popularising tea in Japan.

A Chinese scholar described the magnetic compass a century before Europe — and noticed at once that it doesn't point quite north. Shen Kuo wrote about it in 1088; Europe's first mention dates from 1187.
One elephant bird egg held as much as 160 chicken eggs. At up to 13 litres, these are the largest eggs known from any bird or reptile, dinosaurs included.
The first known European born in the Americas, Greenland aside, was the Icelander Snorri, in Vinland around 1005. His mother Gudrid later made a pilgrimage to Rome.
An Icelandic lawspeaker lost his job because his voice was too weak. He had to recite the law from memory at the Althing, a third each summer — and Grímr Svertingsson simply could not be heard.

The first known reference to hops as a beer preservative is thought to come from a nun: Hildegard of Bingen, in her 12th-century book on healing plants. She also composed music and invented a language.
Legend says El Cid won a battle after he died. When he died in besieged Valencia in 1099, his wife had his body armoured and set on his horse Babieca to rally his troops.
The Bayeux Tapestry is not a tapestry but an embroidery: nearly 70 metres of wool stitched on linen telling the story of the Norman Conquest, Halley's Comet included.
Around 1010, at opposite ends of Asia, two summits of world literature appeared almost at once: Ferdowsi's Persian epic, the Shahnameh, and The Tale of Genji by the Japanese court lady Murasaki.

The grave of Genghis Khan, founder of the largest contiguous empire in history, has never been found. He was buried in secret in 1227, and legend says the site was hidden so that no one could ever find it.
At its height the Mongol Empire was almost one and a half times the size of modern Russia. Around 1279 it covered some 24 million km², the largest contiguous empire in history.
Marco Polo's book was written down by someone else: his cellmate. Captured by Genoa in 1298, Polo told his tales of China to Rustichello da Pisa, a writer of romances, who put them on paper.
While Marco Polo served Kublai Khan in China, a monk from Beijing toured Europe. In 1287 Rabban Bar Sauma met the kings of France and England, and in 1288 the Pope.

For decades scientists saw traces of one of the biggest eruptions in thousands of years in Greenland and Antarctic ice without knowing where the volcano was. Only in 2013 was it found: Samalas on Lombok, 1257.
Chroniclers say that when the Mongols took Baghdad in 1258, the Tigris ran black with ink. So many books from the city's libraries, including the House of Wisdom, were thrown into it.
The founder of Majapahit won with the help of Kublai Khan's army, then drove it out. In 1293 Raden Wijaya got the Mongol force on Java to crush his rival, then turned on the Mongols themselves.

In 1294 Pope Celestine V resigned five months after his election. The hermit, chosen after a two-year conclave, longed to return to his cell, but his successor Boniface VIII kept him in custody until he died.

Murano glass exists because of fear of fire. In 1291 Venice ordered its glassmakers to move their furnaces to the island of Murano so fires would not spread through the wooden city; the island became the world capital of glass.
The original Magna Carta lasted about ten weeks. It was sealed in June 1215, and in August Pope Innocent III declared it void. It became famous through later reissues, such as that of 1225.

The Fibonacci numbers became famous through a puzzle about rabbits. In his Liber Abaci of 1202 Fibonacci asked how many pairs there would be after a year if each pair bred a new pair every month: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8…
Hamelin has a street where music is forbidden. The Pied Piper is said to have led the children down the Bungelosenstraße in 1284, and ever since no instruments are played and no one dances there.

Korean monks carved the Buddhist canon onto 81,258 wooden blocks, and not one error has been found in its 52 million characters. Carved between 1237 and 1248, the blocks are still kept at Haeinsa temple.
New Zealand was the last large landmass people reached. Polynesians arrived around 1280, by which time Oxford had been teaching students for almost 200 years.

The word "assassin" comes from a nickname for the Nizari Ismailis of Alamut. Their targeted killings so alarmed the crusaders that the word entered European languages. In 1256 the fortress surrendered to the Mongols.
Cambridge University is as old as Genghis Khan's empire. Runaway Oxford scholars began teaching in Cambridge in 1209, just three years after Temüjin was proclaimed Genghis Khan.

While England was sealing Magna Carta, whole churches were being cut out of rock in Ethiopia. The churches of Lalibela were carved downward from solid stone in the early 13th century, under King Lalibela.

Yaroslav the Wise is called the 'father-in-law of Europe': three of his daughters became queens. Anne married Henry I of France, Elisiv married Harald Hardrada of Norway, and Anastasia married Andrew I of Hungary.

A queen of France signed her name in Cyrillic. Yaroslav the Wise's daughter Anne married Henry I in 1051, and while regent for her son in the 1060s she signed a charter in Cyrillic letters: 'Ana Reina', Queen Anne.

Yaroslav the Wise's son-in-law died 19 days before the Battle of Hastings. Harald Hardrada of Norway, who had once served in Kiev and married Yaroslav's daughter, invaded England and fell at Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066.
Moscow first appears in the chronicles as the venue for a feast. In 1147 Yuri Dolgoruky invited an ally, 'Come to me, brother, in Moscow', and, the Hypatian Chronicle says, laid on a mighty dinner.

The ominous eclipse in The Tale of Igor's Campaign really happened. On 1 May 1185, as Prince Igor's army marched against the Cumans, a solar eclipse darkened the steppe — astronomers can date it exactly.

The Middle Ages' most famous children's drawings were left by a Novgorod boy named Onfim. Aged six or seven, in the 13th century, he practised letters on birch bark, drew himself as a horseman spearing a foe, and wrote by a beast: 'I am a wild beast'.
The oldest book of Rus was found only in 2000: three wax tablets with psalms from early 11th-century Novgorod. They predate the Ostromir Gospels of 1056–1057, the oldest precisely dated Russian book.
Vikings reached America at about the time Polynesians reached Hawaii. Norsemen were felling trees in Newfoundland in 1021, and radiocarbon dates put the settlement of Hawaii around 1000–1200.

Magna Carta and the Mongol capture of Beijing happened in the same year. In 1215, while English barons were forcing King John to seal the charter, Genghis Khan took Zhongdu, the city on the site of today's Beijing.
New Zealand was settled after work on Notre-Dame had begun. The cathedral's first stone was laid in 1163; Polynesians arrived around 1250–1300, making it the last large landmass people reached.
Europe first saw the fork as a sin. When a Byzantine bride married into the Doge’s family around 1004 and ate with a golden fork, Saint Peter Damian denounced her decadence.

The most elaborate clock of the 11th century stood in China. Su Song’s tower (1088), some 12 metres tall, was driven by a waterwheel and an endless chain, turning an armillary sphere and striking bells.
Al-Jazari's elephant clock put a whole world into one machine: Greek waterworks, an Indian elephant, Chinese dragons, an Egyptian phoenix and the driver's Islamic turban.
It is unclear whether King Harold died from an arrow in the eye. The detail is read into the Bayeux Tapestry, but the figure may not be Harold, and the arrow may have been added during restorations.

The 'Easter Island heads' are full-bodied statues. Many moai on the slopes of Rano Raraku had their torsos buried by centuries of sediment, and excavations have revealed them down to the waist and below.
Marco Polo did not bring pasta back from China. In 1154 the geographer al-Idrisi described dried noodles being made in Sicily and shipped abroad — a century before Polo was born.
